newsitem.title: USA: Simpson jury decision greeted by diverse reaction.
newsitem.headline: Simpson jury decision greeted by diverse reaction.

text.p: The jury verdict against O.J. Simpson in the deaths of his ex-wife and her friend were cheered by some on Tuesday but greeted with scorn by others in a trial that split the nation across racial lines.

"It looks like they nailed him for everything. I felt all along that he was guilty, and I think this is a form of poetic justice. The thing that bothers me is he won't get what he deserves. He won't get jail time," John Robertson, a 57-year-old white man, said at a neighbourhood bar in Pittsburgh.
Added Susan Hank, a 33-year-old white pharmacist visiting the same nightspot: "I think it was the right decision. It took far too long for this to happen."
But Milton Grimes, a black attorney commenting on the trial for ABC-TV, said "I think black people are going to feel here again ... here's another setback. There's a sour taste in my mouth."

Simpson was found innocent of killing his ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman by a largely black jury in a criminal trial 16 months ago. But in the civil case, the largely white jury found him responsible for the deaths.
Asked if the decision would be read by blacks as a case of black and white jurors judging Simpson differently, Grimes said: "Basically that's what happened here."

A black man interviewed at a tavern on the South Side of Chicago told WLS-TV in Chicago "the whole judicial system supported by the white community ... wanted to put him on trial again and find him guilty."

But a black woman at the same bar called the decison "fair" and a white woman at a lounge elsewhere in the city told the same station: "He's gotten away with a lot of things, and now it's come back to haunt him."

The gruesome murders have grabbed the country's attention for more than 2-1/2 years. Simpson's October, 1995, acquittal on criminal murder charges left the once-popular sports hero and celebrity pitchman free but under a cloud of suspicion.

Unlike the 1995 verdict which was televised live from the court room and triggered instant reaction -- heavily divided along racial lines -- the civil trial decision emerged ponderously on TV. It came at the tail end of President Bill Clinton's State of the Union Address, flashed beneath the screen.

Some independent TV stations eschewed the Clinton speech in favour of live coverage from outside the California courthouse where the verdict was announced. A cheer went up in the street outside when news of the verdict spread.

But commercial and cable news networks kept the attention on Clinton, squeezing in a quick summation on the case after Clinton finished speaking and before the Republican party gave its official response.

Albaro Herrera, 33, a passenger service worker at Miami International Airport, said he believed Simpson was guilty and was pleased he was going to pay for the crime, but monetary damages were "not enough."
"Life doesn't have a price. They can't bring those people back to life," Herrera said. "It just means you can kill anyone and then you pay some amount of money and that's it."
Fritz Philippe, 53, a Haitian-American retired teacher from Miami, said he believed the judgment was retribution against Simpson for the first trial.
"I believe that many people weren't happy about the first trial. So they had to make him pay somehow," Philippe said. "If they are out to destroy you, they will get you one way or another."
Lewis, a 42-year-old black property manager who declined to give his last name, said he had thought the jury would find Simpson liable, though he personally believed he was framed.
"American justice isn't totally blind. Had he been a different skin colour they would not have found this way," he said. "It's just a demonstration of the racial attitudes in this country."

Robert Clifford, a civil litigator in Chicago who had predicted more than a week ago that the jury would hold Simpson responsible for the deaths, said several factors influenced the decision including a lesser standard of proof "and a jury that was not probably willing to be persuaded by racial excesses or manipulations."
